title: Tax Delinquent Property List: How to Get and Use Them to Find Real Estate Deals
excerpt: Tax delinquent property lists are one of the most powerful tools for finding motivated sellers before properties hit the open market. Learn exactly how to get these lists, what to do with them, and how to turn unpaid taxes into profitable real estate deals.

sections.content: Some of the best real estate deals never appear on Zillow or the MLS. They come from a source most investors overlook: the county tax office. A tax delinquent property list shows you exactly which homeowners have fallen behind on their property taxes — and those homeowners are often desperate to sell. If you want to consistently find off-market deals, learning how to get and use these lists is a skill worth mastering. It fits neatly into a broader strategy for finding motivated sellers, which you can explore in our [How to Find Motivated Sellers: Complete Guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/finding-motivated-sellers).
What Is a Tax Delinquent Property List?

When a property owner stops paying their local property taxes, the county government records that delinquency. After a certain period — usually one to three years depending on the state — the county can begin the process of seizing the property through a tax lien sale or a tax deed sale. Before that happens, the county compiles a list of every property in default. That is the tax delinquent property list. It typically includes the owner's name, the property address, the parcel number, and the total amount of back taxes owed. In high-delinquency markets like [Detroit, MI](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/detroit-mi), [Memphis, TN](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/memphis-tn), and [St. Louis, MO](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/st-louis-mo), these lists can contain thousands of properties at any given time.
Why Tax Delinquent Properties Make Great Leads

A homeowner who is not paying their property taxes is usually dealing with a bigger financial or personal problem. They may have lost their job, inherited a property they cannot afford to maintain, gone through a divorce, or simply given up on a house that needs too many repairs. That financial pressure creates motivation to sell — and motivated sellers are where real estate investors find their best margins. Unlike homeowners who are casually testing the market, a tax-delinquent owner often needs a real solution fast. They are not waiting for top dollar. They want out.
The best deals in real estate are made before the property ever hits the market. Tax delinquent lists give you a direct line to homeowners who need help — before everyone else knows they're selling.
How to Get a Tax Delinquent Property List
Step 1: Contact Your County Tax Assessor or Treasurer

The tax delinquent list is a public record in most states. Start by calling or visiting the website of your county tax assessor, county treasurer, or county auditor — the office name varies by location. Ask specifically for the delinquent tax roll or the delinquent property list. Many counties now publish this information online in a searchable database or as a downloadable spreadsheet. Others require a formal public records request. Some counties charge a small fee, typically $10 to $50, for a full data export.
Step 2: Look for Published Tax Lien and Tax Sale Notices

In many states, counties are legally required to publish delinquent tax notices in local newspapers before a tax sale. These notices are often published four to eight weeks before the auction and list every property scheduled for sale. You can find these in your local legal newspaper or on the county's official website. This is actually an ideal time to contact owners — they are staring down a deadline and may be more willing to negotiate quickly.
Step 3: Use a Data Provider for Larger Scale

If you are working multiple counties or want a cleaner, skip-traced dataset, third-party data providers can save you significant time. Services like PropStream, ATTOM, and BatchLeads aggregate county-level delinquent tax data and append it with phone numbers and mailing addresses. Expect to pay $100 to $500 per month depending on your data volume needs. For investors just getting started, pulling lists directly from the county is free and a great way to learn the process before spending on tools.

Pro Tip: When you pull your list, filter for properties where taxes have been delinquent for two or more years. These owners have had longer to accumulate financial pressure and are often more motivated than someone who just missed one payment.
How to Use a Tax Delinquent Property List Effectively
Clean and Filter Your List First

A raw delinquent tax list can contain hundreds or thousands of entries. Not every property is worth pursuing. Before you start marketing, filter out vacant lots, commercial properties (unless that is your focus), and properties with more delinquent taxes than the deal could support. Also remove any properties already in bankruptcy proceedings, as those require a different legal process. After filtering, you might find that 20 to 30 percent of the original list represents real opportunities.
Run a Quick Deal Analysis Before Reaching Out

Before you spend time and money marketing to a list, do a rough numbers check. Look up the property's estimated value using recent comparable sales, estimate the repair costs based on the property's condition, and calculate whether there is enough room for a deal. Use our free [Deal Calculator](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator) to quickly run the numbers and confirm whether a property fits your buying criteria. A property with $15,000 in back taxes, $40,000 in repairs, and a $90,000 ARV probably has room for a deal. One with $8,000 in back taxes and a $400,000 ARV in a hot neighborhood might not need your help at all.
Choose Your Outreach Method

Direct mail is the most common approach for tax delinquent lists and for good reason — these owners are not always reachable by phone and a physical letter signals that you are serious. Send a simple, genuine letter explaining that you buy houses in any condition and that you can close quickly. Avoid sounding like a form letter. Personalize it with the property address and a handwritten signature if possible. Many investors send three to five mailers to the same list over 60 to 90 days because response rates improve with repetition. Cold calling and text messaging can also work well once you have phone numbers appended to your list.

items: Direct mail: Cost-effective and scalable, best for larger lists
Cold calling: Higher touch, faster feedback, requires skip-traced numbers
Door knocking: High conversion rate but time-intensive, pairs well with driving for dollars
Text messaging: Fast and affordable but check your state's regulations carefully
Email: Lower open rates for homeowners but useful for investor-to-investor deals

sections.content: Combine Tax Delinquent Lists With Other Lead Sources

The most successful investors stack multiple lead sources to find the highest-motivated sellers. A property that appears on both a tax delinquent list and a code violation list is a very strong signal — the owner is not paying taxes and not maintaining the home. You can learn how to pull those public records in our article on [Code Violation Lists: Finding Sellers From City Records](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/code-violation-property-list). Similarly, if a property on your delinquent tax list also shows signs of vacancy when you drive the neighborhood, that is another layer of motivation. Our guide on the [Best Driving for Dollars Apps Compared (2026)](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/best-driving-for-dollars-apps) can help you identify distressed properties in person. You can also cross-reference with divorce filings, which are another powerful signal of financial distress — see our guide on [Divorce and Real Estate: Finding Motivated Sellers Ethically](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/divorce-motivated-seller-leads).
Real-World Example: How the Numbers Can Work

Imagine you pull a delinquent tax list in Memphis, TN and identify a three-bedroom house with $9,500 in back taxes owed. The owner inherited the home two years ago, has not been able to afford repairs, and wants to avoid a tax sale. You estimate the ARV at $110,000 with $25,000 in needed repairs. Using the standard 70 percent rule, your maximum offer would be around $52,000. You negotiate a deal at $48,000, assign the contract to a local flipper for a $7,000 assignment fee, and close in three weeks. The seller avoids losing the home at a tax auction for pennies. The buyer gets a renovation project with solid upside. You earn $7,000 for finding the deal. That is exactly how tax delinquent lists are meant to work. If you are new to deal structures like assignment contracts, the [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) guide is a great place to start, and you can sharpen your analysis skills with our [How to Analyze Real Estate Deals](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/how-to-analyze-real-estate-deals) guide.

Pro Tip: Always approach tax-delinquent sellers with empathy. They are often dealing with a difficult situation. Investors who lead with helpfulness — offering a real solution rather than a lowball pitch — consistently get better responses and close more deals.
Common Mistakes to Avoid

items: Skipping the deal analysis and wasting marketing money on unprofitable properties
Only mailing once — most responses come on the second or third touchpoint
Ignoring properties with large amounts of back taxes — sometimes those are the most motivated sellers
Forgetting to check for additional liens beyond back taxes, such as HOA liens or code violation fines
Not following up quickly when a seller responds — motivated sellers talk to multiple investors
Being too aggressive or transactional in your messaging — empathy converts better
